extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent applicants and practitioners (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and formulating rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (patent subject-matter eligibility), including how to identify judicial exceptions, perform the Step 2A/2B (Alice/Mayo) analysis, evaluate applicant responses, and clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature rejection requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim as a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited in the claim (i.e., set forth or described) and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the comparison to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (e.g., isolated X vs X in natural state). Cite MPEP § 2106.04(b) (products of nature) and MPEP § 2106.04(c) (markedly different characteristics analysis). Provide a sample explanation demonstrating identification of recited exception and rationale (structure, function, properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional claim elements do not add significantly more (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address additional elements both individually and as a combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Note that a new combination may be patent eligible even though each step was known individually (Diamond v. Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify or not as 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection only when readily apparent to examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to claiming significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Conversely, when appropriate, explain why additional elements provide an inventive concept by meaningfully limiting the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain conventionality with reasoned rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the rejection should explain why courts or those in the relevant field would recognize those claim limitations as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation supporting the conclusion that the element is well-understood, routine, conventional. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for more on well-understood, routine, conventional activities and elements; consider citing examples or sources when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components/functionality guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2106.05(d) lists computer functions courts have recognized as well-understood/routine when claimed generically. Do not assume all computer functions are conventional; assess whether generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more on generic computing functions as mere instructions to implement an exception on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data) or merely link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment/field of use generally do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples (storing data after computing a mathematical relationship does not add meaningful limitation; limiting to particular industry insufficient per Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(g) for insignificant extra-solution activity and § 2106.05(h) for field-of-use linking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: suggest claim elements to overcome rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection, it is best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action as suggested ways to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification discloses elements that would make the claim significantly more, point them out to applicant as potential narrowing/amendment options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for identifying judicial exceptions (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing Step 2A, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception recited in the claim and explaining why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on external evidence to find a claim is directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts typically treat eligibility as a question of law and often identify exceptions by comparing claimed subject matter to precedent without requiring evidence (cases cited: Rapid Litig. Mgmt., OIP Techs., Content Extraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for Step 2B (significantly more)
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the claim does not recite significantly more than the judicial exception (e.g., that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if available, sources of evidence can be provided to support the assertion or to rebut applicant arguments. The specification's statements that elements are conventional may be used. Other evidence could include manuals, handbooks, prior patents, or court decisions describing conventionality or state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in citing case law as evidence of conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing case law to support a finding of conventionality, ensure that the facts of the cited case comport with the facts of the application being examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should be familiar with the facts of the cases they cite. Examples: Content Extraction (scanner use was well-known), Versata (basic computer functions). Use case law supported rationale rather than unsupported citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's response to §101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: After issuing a §101 rejection, examiners must carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence rebutting the subject matter eligibility rejection; if the applicant amends, determine the amended claim’s broadest reasonable interpretation and re-perform the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If amendments/arguments persuasively establish eligibility, withdraw the rejection. Applicant may amend or present persuasive arguments/evidence in good faith. Consider combination of elements and whether individual or combined elements amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as 'significantly more' (examples of qualifying limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element may qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the judicial exception, e.g., it improves another technology or technical field, improves functioning of a computer itself, adds a specific limitation beyond well-understood routine activity, or adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an element is generic individually, it can amount to significantly more when combined with other elements. Generic components in combination may perform non-generic functions and thus be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required rebuttal when maintaining rejection after applicant challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings but the examiner deems it appropriate to maintain the rejection, a rebuttal must be provided in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate responses include: (1) explaining why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to a concept in a cited case (and cite a supporting case if one was not previously cited), (2) reevaluating if applicant provides evidence that additional elements are not well-understood/routine and considering providing evidence if maintaining the rejection, (3) analyzing whether adding a generic computer or 'specially programmed' computer supplies significantly more (mere addition is insufficient), (4) reconsidering Step 2A/2B if applicant argues claim specificity or lack of preemption, including whether claim improves computer functioning or technical field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when claims are eligible or when issuing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record describing which specification portions support the claimed improvement and which claim elements produce that improvement; clarifying remarks may also be useful to explain the rationale for a rejection (e.g., explain the BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks can be made during prosecution or at notice of allowance. Example: explaining that the BRI of a computer-readable-medium claim covers a carrier wave and suggesting narrowing amendments to overcome a §101 rejection.
